items.prompt: Give a one-minute talk about your favourite place in Indonesia. Say where it is, what you can do there and why you like it.

criteria.label: Speaks clearly at a steady pace
Gives at least three details about the place
Explains why they like it
Has a clear beginning and ending

hints: Plan three points: where it is, what you do there and why you like it.
Start with a greeting and finish with a sentence that sums up.
items.explanation: A short talk is easy to follow when it has a clear opening, three main points and an ending.

items.prompt: Read the passage aloud. Change your voice for each character and show their feelings.

criteria.label: Reads the words accurately
Uses different voices for Tika, her brother and Grandpa
Pauses at full stops and commas
Shows feelings such as excitement and surprise

items.readText:
“Quick, hide!” whispered Tika. Footsteps were coming up the stairs. Her little brother squeezed behind the curtain, giggling.
“Shh! Do you want Grandpa to find us?” she hissed.
The door creaked open. For a long moment, nobody moved. Then a deep voice boomed, “I wonder where my two grandchildren are. What a shame. I suppose I will have to eat all these pancakes myself!”
The curtain gave a squeak. Tika’s brother had already run out.
hints: Read it silently first and decide how each character sounds.
Whispered words should be quiet. Boomed words should be loud and deep.
items.explanation: Reading with expression means changing your voice to match the characters and their feelings, and pausing at punctuation.

items.prompt: Explain how to play a game you know well to a child in Grade 1. Use simple words and short steps.

criteria.label: Uses simple words a young child would understand
Explains the steps in a clear order
Checks understanding, for example by asking a question
Speaks kindly and clearly

hints: Pick a simple game, such as hide and seek or a clapping game.
Use order words: first, next, then, finally.
items.explanation: When you speak to a younger child, use short sentences, simple words and a friendly voice, and check that they understand.

items.prompt: Persuade your class to join a club you would like to start at school. Ask the audience at least one question.

criteria.label: States clearly what the club is
Gives at least two good reasons to join
Asks the audience a question to involve them
Sounds confident and enthusiastic
Ends by telling the audience what to do next

hints: A question such as Have you ever wanted to... grabs attention.
Finish with a clear instruction, such as where and when to sign up.
items.explanation: A persuasive talk grabs attention, gives reasons, speaks to the audience directly and tells them what to do next.

items.prompt: Imagine you are reading the news on the school radio. Report one piece of good news from your school or neighbourhood.

criteria.label: Says who, what, where and when
Uses a clear, formal newsreader voice
Includes a short comment from someone involved
Finishes within ninety seconds

hints: Begin with the most important fact, just like a newspaper headline.
Keep your voice steady and clear, like a real newsreader.
items.explanation: A news report on the radio gives the main facts first, in a clear and formal voice, and may include what someone involved said.

items.prompt: Retell a folk tale you know, such as the mouse-deer and the crocodiles, in your own words. Keep it under two minutes.

criteria.label: Tells the events in the right order
Uses time words such as one day, then and finally
Uses expression and different voices for characters
Speaks to the listener as if telling the story to a friend
Ends the story clearly

hints: Before you start, list the main events on your fingers.
Make the clever character and the tricked character sound different.
items.explanation: A good retelling keeps the events in order, uses time words and brings the characters to life with your voice.

items.prompt: You are giving a talk to Grade 1 children about looking after their teeth. Which sentence suits them best?

options.text: Brush your teeth twice a day, so they stay strong and shiny.
Dental hygiene is essential for preventing tooth decay.
options.why: These words are too difficult for young children.

options.text: Whatever, just brush them or not.
options.why: This is too casual and does not help the children.

options.text: Fluoride makes tooth enamel harder and stronger.
options.why: Young children would not understand these scientific words.

hints: Think about the age of your audience.
Young children need short sentences and everyday words.
Read each option and imagine a six-year-old hearing it.
items.explanation: For young children, use short sentences and simple words. The correct option tells them what to do and why in words they know.

items.prompt: In a group discussion, which is the most polite way to disagree?

options.text: That’s a silly idea.
options.why: This could hurt your classmate’s feelings.

options.text: No. You’re wrong.
options.why: This is rude and does not explain your view.

options.text: I see what you mean, but I think there is another way to look at it.
Stop talking so I can speak.
options.why: Everyone should get a turn, and this is unkind.

hints: Polite disagreement respects the other person’s idea.
Look for an answer that shows you listened before giving your view.
Ask: which sentence would make a classmate want to keep talking with you?
items.explanation: Saying I see what you mean shows you listened. Then you can share your own view without hurting anyone’s feelings.

items.prompt: Which is the best way to start a presentation?

options.text: Um, so, yeah, orangutans.
options.why: This sounds unprepared and does not greet the audience.

options.text: The end. Any questions?
options.why: This is how you finish, not how you start.

options.text: I don’t really want to do this.
options.why: This makes the audience less interested.

options.text: Good morning, everyone. Today I am going to tell you about orangutans.

hints: A good start greets the audience.
The start should also tell the audience what the talk is about.
Find the option with a greeting and a topic.
items.explanation: A good opening greets the audience and tells them the topic, so they know what to listen for.

items.prompt: Give a one-minute speech for or against this idea: Pupils should choose their own homework. Give a reason, an example and an answer to the other side.

criteria.label: States clearly whether they are for or against
Gives a reason with an example
Answers a point the other side might make
Uses linking phrases such as firstly, however and to sum up
Speaks confidently, with a strong final sentence

hints: Decide your side first, then think of your best reason.
Imagine what someone on the other side would say, and plan a polite answer.
items.explanation: A strong debate speech states a clear position, supports it with reasons and examples and answers the other side politely.

items.prompt: Which helps your audience hear your talk well?

options.text: Speaking quietly to the floor
options.why: The audience will not hear you.

options.text: Speaking clearly at a steady pace
Speaking as fast as you can
options.why: Fast speech is hard to follow.

options.text: Whispering the whole time
options.why: The audience cannot hear a whisper.

hints: Think about the people at the back.
Clear and steady helps.
Pick the option that is easy to hear.
items.explanation: Clear, steady speech helps everyone understand your talk.

items.prompt: Sort these habits into good presenting habits and habits to avoid.

items.text: Speak clearly and not too fast
Read every word from the paper
Turn your back to the audience

hints: Imagine being in the audience.
Which habits help people follow?
Which would make you stop listening?
items.explanation: Eye contact, clear speech and pauses help the audience, while mumbling and reading everything do not.

items.prompt: Put the steps for preparing a talk in order.
hints: You prepare before you speak.
Notes come after the topic.
Questions come at the end.
items.explanation: Prepare first, practise, give the talk, and answer questions last.

items.prompt: Which opening would best grab attention in a talk about recycling?

options.text: Today I will talk about recycling.
options.why: This is plain and does not grab attention.

options.text: Did you know that one plastic bottle can take over four hundred years to break down?
Recycling is a topic.
options.why: This is dull and gives no interest.

options.text: I did not prepare much.
options.why: This weakens your talk.

hints: A good opening makes the audience curious.
A surprising fact or question works well.
Which option makes you want to listen?
items.explanation: A question and a surprising fact make people want to listen.

items.prompt: Which slide is best for a talk to a class?

options.text: A whole page of small sentences
options.why: Too much text to read.

options.text: A title, three short points and a clear picture
Only a long paragraph
options.why: Too much text.

options.text: A blank slide
options.why: No help to the audience.

hints: Slides support the speaker.
Less text is easier to read.
Choose short points with a picture.
items.explanation: A few short points and a picture are easy to read while you speak.

items.prompt: You cannot answer a question after your talk. Choose 2 good ways to respond.

options.text: Say honestly that you are not sure.
Make up an answer quickly.
Offer to find out and tell them later.
Laugh at the question.
Ignore the person.

hints: Honesty is important.
Be polite.
Which options respect the person asking?
items.explanation: Being honest and offering to find out is polite and trustworthy.

items.prompt: What do we call a short stop in your talk that lets the audience think? Write one word.
hints: It is silent.
It helps the audience think.
It starts with p.
items.explanation: A pause lets the audience take in an important point.

items.prompt: Build a polite ending for a talk.
items.answer: Thank you for listening to my talk.
hints: Start with thanks.
Use the word listening.
It ends with talk.
items.explanation: Thanking the audience is a polite way to end.

items.prompt: Match each speaking skill to what it does.
pairs: Shows you are talking to the audience
Lets people at the back hear you
Hand movements that support your words
hints: Think about what each word means.
Volume is about loudness.
Pace is about speed.
items.explanation: Each skill helps the audience understand and stay interested.

items.prompt: Which shows active listening in a group discussion?

options.text: Looking at your phone while others talk
options.why: This shows you are not listening.

options.text: Nodding, and then asking a question about what Maya said
Talking over the speaker
options.why: This is rude.

options.text: Waiting for your turn without paying attention
options.why: You must pay attention.

hints: Active listening means you pay attention.
Show you heard the speaker.
Which option links to what was said?
items.explanation: Nodding and asking about what the speaker said shows you have really listened.

items.prompt: A friend says you spoke too fast in your talk. What is the best response?

options.text: Speak even faster next time.
options.why: This makes it worse.

options.text: Practise with pauses and slow down.
Give up talking.
options.why: This does not help you improve.

options.text: Say the friend is wrong.
options.why: Feedback helps you.

hints: Feedback helps you improve.
What would fix speaking too fast?
Choose the helpful action.
items.explanation: Slowing down and adding pauses will help the audience follow.

items.prompt: Sort each phrase by where it suits best.

items.text: I would like to thank our teachers.
Today I will explain our garden.

hints: Formal talks use polite, full phrases.
Friends use casual words.
Gonna is informal.
items.explanation: A formal talk uses polite complete phrases, while a chat uses casual words.

items.prompt: Which sentence is most persuasive in a speech asking everyone to join a tree-planting day?

options.text: We might plant trees.
options.why: Too weak.

options.text: Trees are green.
options.why: A fact, but not persuasive.

options.text: Imagine our school yard shaded by trees: will you help make it happen on Saturday?
Trees exist.
options.why: Too weak.

hints: Persuasive speech uses a vivid picture and asks for action.
Which option uses a question?
Which makes the audience feel involved?
items.explanation: The vivid picture and the direct question invite the audience to act.

items.prompt: You have two minutes and your audience is getting restless. Which plan is best?

options.text: Read a long script in one flat voice.
options.why: This would bore the audience.

options.text: Start with a question, give three key points with a short example, then finish by summing up.
Talk about everything you know.
options.why: Too long and unfocused.

options.text: Speak quietly so they must listen.
options.why: They will not hear you.

hints: Two minutes is short.
Keep it clear and lively.
Choose a plan with a hook, a few points and a close.
items.explanation: A hook, three focused points and a summary keep a short talk lively and easy to follow.

items.prompt: Choose all the ways that make reading a story aloud more exciting.

options.text: Change your pace at a tense moment.
Use different voices for characters.
Read in one flat tone.
Whisper at a secret.
Read as fast as possible.

hints: Use your voice to show feelings.
Variety keeps listeners interested.
Flat and rushed reading is hard to enjoy.
items.explanation: Changing pace, voices and volume brings a story to life.
